definition: A small number showing how many times to multiply a base number by itself.
whyItMatters: Exponents explain how populations, viral videos, and computer memory grow fast.

definition: A whole number greater than 1 that can only be divided evenly by 1 and itself.
example: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 are primes; 12 is not because 3 × 4 = 12.
whyItMatters: Huge prime numbers protect online passwords and banking encryption.

definition: A sequence where each number is the sum of the two numbers right before it.
whyItMatters: Fibonacci spirals show up in pinecones, sunflowers, and sea shells.

definition: Multiplying a whole number by every positive whole number smaller than it.
example: 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways to line up 4 books.
whyItMatters: Factorials count how many ways cards, chess pieces, or passwords can be arranged.

definition: A comparison showing how much of one quantity there is compared to another.
example: A 2:1 ratio of flour to water means 2 cups of flour for every 1 cup of water.
whyItMatters: Cooking recipes, map scales, and screen resolutions all rely on ratios.

definition: The ratio of any circle's distance around the edge to its width across the middle.
example: A circle 10 cm wide has a circumference of about 31.4 cm.
whyItMatters: Engineers use pi to design wheels, pipes, satellites, and stadium domes.

definition: A number that, when multiplied by itself, gives the original number.
example: The square root of 49 is 7 because 7 × 7 = 49.
whyItMatters: Square roots help calculate diagonal distances and physics formulas.

definition: A flat closed shape made of straight line segments.
example: Triangles, squares, pentagons, and hexagons are all polygons.
whyItMatters: 3D video games build characters and worlds out of thousands of tiny polygons.

definition: The total distance all the way around the outside of a flat shape.
example: A soccer field 100 m long and 60 m wide has a perimeter of 320 m.
whyItMatters: You need perimeter to measure fencing, picture frames, and running tracks.

definition: The amount of flat space inside a 2D shape, measured in square units.
example: A room 4 m by 5 m has an area of 20 square meters.
whyItMatters: Area tells you how much paint, carpet, or solar panels will fit on a surface.

definition: The amount of 3D space inside a solid object or container.
example: A fish tank 50 × 30 × 40 cm holds 60,000 cubic cm (60 liters).
whyItMatters: Volume measures everything from water bottles to cargo ships.

definition: A number that represents equal parts of a whole.
example: Eating 3 slices of an 8-slice pizza means you ate 3/8.
whyItMatters: Fractions are essential for music beats, baking, and splitting bills.

definition: A fraction out of 100, written with the % sign.
example: 25% of 80 points is 20 points.
whyItMatters: Discounts, battery levels, and test grades all use percentages.

definition: When one half of a shape or pattern is a mirror image of the other half.
example: A butterfly's left and right wings have line symmetry.
whyItMatters: Symmetry helps architects balance buildings and nature build crystals.

definition: Any whole number—positive, negative, or zero—with no fractions or decimals.
example: -5, 0, and 42 are integers; 3.5 is not.
whyItMatters: Elevators, bank balances, and temperatures below freezing use negative integers.

definition: How far a number is from zero on the number line, always positive or zero.
example: Both |-7| and |7| equal 7.
whyItMatters: Absolute value measures distance or error without caring about direction.

definition: Two lines on a flat surface that stay the exact same distance apart and never meet.
example: Straight train tracks run parallel to each other.
whyItMatters: Parallel lines keep shelves level and skyscrapers standing straight.

definition: Two lines that meet at an exact 90-degree right angle.
example: The corner of a book page forms perpendicular edges.
whyItMatters: Builders use right angles to make sturdy walls and doors.

definition: The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the 90-degree angle.
example: In a 3-4-5 right triangle, 5 is the hypotenuse.
whyItMatters: Helps surveyors and GPS systems find straight-line distances.

definition: In a right triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side.
whyItMatters: One of the most used formulas in construction, navigation, and game physics.

definition: A number showing how steep a line is, found by dividing vertical rise by horizontal run.
example: A ramp rising 2 meters over 10 meters has a slope of 0.2.
whyItMatters: Road signs, ski runs, and wheelchair ramps are designed using slope.

definition: A 2D grid formed by a horizontal x-axis and a vertical y-axis.
example: The point (3, 4) is 3 steps right and 4 steps up from (0, 0).
whyItMatters: Every pixel on your screen and every player on a game map uses coordinates.

definition: A letter or symbol that stands for a number that can change or is unknown.
example: In x + 5 = 12, the variable x equals 7.
whyItMatters: Variables let one formula work for millions of different situations.

definition: A math statement showing two expressions are equal using an = sign.
example: 3 × n = 15 is an equation solved by n = 5.
whyItMatters: Equations let scientists model everything from rocket launches to savings.

definition: A math statement comparing two values that are not equal, using <, >, ≤, or ≥.
example: Height ≥ 140 cm to ride the roller coaster.
whyItMatters: Budgets, speed limits, and safety rules are all inequalities.

definition: A whole number that divides evenly into another number with no remainder.
example: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.
whyItMatters: Factors help simplify fractions and split teams evenly.

definition: The result of multiplying a number by any whole number.
example: Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30...
whyItMatters: Multiples help line up repeating schedules like bus arrivals.

definition: A whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors.
example: 9 is composite because it divides by 1, 3, and 9.
whyItMatters: Every composite number can be broken down into unique prime building blocks.

definition: The largest whole number that divides evenly into two or more numbers.
example: For 18 and 24, the greatest common divisor is 6.
whyItMatters: Used to reduce fractions to their simplest form.

definition: The smallest positive number that is a multiple of two or more numbers.
example: For 4 and 6, the least common multiple is 12.
whyItMatters: Helps add fractions with different denominators and sync repeating events.

definition: Replacing a number with a nearby simpler value to make it easier to use.
example: Rounding 48.7 to the nearest whole number gives 49.
whyItMatters: Quick mental estimates at the store use rounding.

definition: Finding a close-enough answer quickly without doing exact arithmetic.
example: Estimating 19 × 21 as 20 × 20 = 400.
whyItMatters: Estimation catches calculator typos before they cause mistakes.

definition: A number system based on powers of 10 using a dot to show parts smaller than 1.
example: 0.75 means 75 hundredths, or 3/4.
whyItMatters: Money, metric measurements, and race times use decimals.

definition: A compact way to write huge or tiny numbers using powers of 10.
example: 300,000,000 is written as 3 × 10⁸.
whyItMatters: Astronomers use it for star distances without writing dozens of zeros.

definition: The inverse of an exponent—it asks what power gives a target number.
example: log₁₀(1000) = 3 because 10³ = 1000.
whyItMatters: Earthquake scales and sound decibels use logarithms.

definition: A straight line passing through the center of a circle from edge to edge.
example: A pizza 30 cm wide has a diameter of 30 cm.
whyItMatters: Bike wheels, pipes, and coins are sized by diameter.

definition: The distance from the center of a circle to any point on its edge.
example: A circle with diameter 20 cm has a radius of 10 cm.
whyItMatters: Used to measure blast zones, Wi-Fi range, and wheel size.

definition: The total distance around the outer edge of a circle.
example: A circle with diameter 10 cm has circumference ≈ 31.4 cm.
whyItMatters: Determines how far a bicycle rolls in one wheel turn.

definition: An angle measuring less than 90 degrees.
example: A 45-degree corner of a slice of pizza is acute.
whyItMatters: Roof trusses and arrowheads use sharp acute angles.

definition: An angle measuring more than 90 degrees and less than 180 degrees.
example: An open laptop screen tilted back to 120 degrees forms an obtuse angle.
whyItMatters: Reclining chairs and boomerang wings use obtuse angles.

definition: An exact 90-degree angle, like the corner of a square.
example: A clock at 3:00 shows a right angle between its hands.
whyItMatters: Keeps floors flat and walls upright.

definition: Shapes that have the exact same size and shape, even if rotated or flipped.
example: Two identical puzzle pieces are congruent.
whyItMatters: Factories rely on congruent parts so replacements always fit.

definition: Shapes with the exact same angles and proportions, but possibly different sizes.
example: A toy car and a real 1:24 scale car are similar.
whyItMatters: Maps, architectural models, and photo zooming use similarity.

definition: Covering a flat surface completely with repeating shapes that leave no gaps or overlaps.
example: Honeycomb hexagons and brick walls are tessellations.
whyItMatters: Artists and tile makers use tessellations for seamless patterns.

definition: A never-ending pattern that looks similar at both giant and microscopic scales.
example: A fern leaf's tiny branches look like miniature versions of the whole leaf.
whyItMatters: Fractals help model coastlines, clouds, and tree branches.

definition: A special number around 1.618 that appears when a line is split in a balanced proportion.
example: A rectangle 16.18 cm by 10 cm has sides in the golden ratio.
whyItMatters: Artists and designers have used this proportion for centuries.

definition: A well-defined collection of distinct objects or numbers.
example: {2, 4, 6, 8} is the set of even numbers under 10.
whyItMatters: Database queries and search filters work by combining sets.

definition: The elements that belong to both of two sets at the same time.
example: The intersection of {1,2,3} and {2,3,4} is {2,3}.
whyItMatters: Search engines use intersection when you search two words together.

definition: All elements combined from two or more sets, without duplicates.
example: The union of {1,2} and {2,3} is {1,2,3}.
whyItMatters: Used when merging lists or combining user groups.

definition: Overlapping circles used to show how sets share or differ in elements.
example: Circle A for soccer players, Circle B for swimmers, overlap for both.
whyItMatters: Makes comparing categories instant to see.

definition: An arrangement of items where the exact order matters.
example: 123 and 321 are two different permutations of the digits 1, 2, 3.
whyItMatters: Used for locker combinations and race podiums.

definition: A selection of items where the order does not matter.
example: Picking pepperoni and mushrooms on a pizza is the same as mushrooms and pepperoni.
whyItMatters: Helps count card hands and team rosters.

definition: A concept describing something larger than any finite number, with no end.
example: There is no largest whole number because you can always add 1.
whyItMatters: Infinity is key to calculus, geometry, and understanding the universe.

definition: The number representing nothing, or the boundary between positive and negative numbers.
whyItMatters: Place-value math and all modern computers could not exist without zero.

definition: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign.
example: -10°C is 10 degrees colder than freezing.
whyItMatters: Tracks debt, elevation below sea level, and countdowns.

definition: One divided by a number—flipping a fraction upside down.
example: The reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3, and 3/4 × 4/3 = 1.
whyItMatters: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

definition: The agreed rule (PEMDAS/BODMAS) for which math step to do first.
example: In 2 + 3 × 4, multiply first to get 2 + 12 = 14.
whyItMatters: Ensures everyone and every computer gets the exact same answer.

definition: Multiplying a sum by a number gives the same result as multiplying each part separately.
whyItMatters: Makes mental multiplication of big numbers fast and easy.

definition: Changing the order of numbers in addition or multiplication does not change the result.
whyItMatters: Lets you rearrange calculations into easier pairs.

definition: Changing how numbers are grouped with parentheses in addition or multiplication keeps the same result.
whyItMatters: Helps group numbers into friendly tens.

definition: The result of multiplying a whole number by itself three times.
whyItMatters: Used to compute the volume of boxes and 3D grids.

definition: The result of multiplying a whole number by itself.
whyItMatters: Forms the basis for grid areas and chessboards (8² = 64 squares).

definition: A math rule that takes an input and produces exactly one output.
example: If f(x) = 2x + 1, then f(4) = 9.
whyItMatters: Both algebra and computer programming are built around functions.

definition: An equation whose graph forms a straight line.
example: y = 2x + 3 rises by 2 every time x increases by 1.
whyItMatters: Models constant speeds, hourly pay, and simple prices.

definition: A U-shaped curve created by squaring a variable, like y = x².
example: A basketball arc or water fountain stream follows a parabola.
whyItMatters: Satellite dishes use parabolic curves to focus signals.

definition: A perfectly round 3D ball where every surface point is the same distance from the center.
example: A soccer ball or globe is shaped like a sphere.
whyItMatters: Gravity pulls planets and stars into spheres.

definition: A 3D shape with two parallel circular ends joined by a curved side.
example: A soup can or AA battery is a cylinder.
whyItMatters: Engines, pipes, and storage tanks use cylinders for strength.

definition: A 3D shape with a flat circular base that tapers smoothly to a single point.
example: An ice cream cone or traffic cone.
whyItMatters: Nose cones on rockets reduce air drag.

definition: A 3D solid made of flat polygon faces with straight edges and sharp corners.
example: A cube (6 faces) and a pyramid (5 faces) are polyhedra.
whyItMatters: Board game dice and crystal structures are polyhedra.

definition: A corner point where two or more lines or edges meet.
example: A triangle has 3 vertices; a cube has 8 vertices.
whyItMatters: 3D graphics store objects as lists of vertices.

definition: A rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns.
example: A 2×2 matrix holds 4 numbers in 2 rows and 2 columns.
whyItMatters: Video games and AI neural networks run billions of matrix operations.

definition: A quantity that has both size (magnitude) and direction.
example: Wind blowing 30 km/h toward the north is a vector.
whyItMatters: Game physics, airplanes, and robotics rely on vectors.

definition: An operation that finds the remainder after dividing one whole number by another.
example: 17 mod 5 = 2 because 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.
whyItMatters: Clock arithmetic (14:00 = 2 PM) and cryptography use modulo.

definition: A number triangle where each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.
whyItMatters: Quickly gives combinations and powers of binomials.

definition: The study of networks made of dots (nodes) connected by lines (edges).
example: A subway map showing stations and rail lines is a graph.
whyItMatters: GPS navigation and social networks run on graph theory.
